notes.h: Why fruit and vegetables lose nutrients
notes.b: Not every nutrient in fruit and vegetables is equally fragile. Some are easily lost in preparation and cooking, and others are hardly affected, so the guidelines are aimed at protecting the fragile ones.
points: Vitamin C and the B vitamins (thiamine, riboflavin and folate) are water-soluble, so they dissolve into any water the food touches. They are also damaged by heat and by oxygen in the air.
Vitamin C is the least stable of these vitamins, so it is the one the guidelines work hardest to protect.
Minerals dissolve in water too, so they leach out (seep out into the water) when vegetables are soaked or boiled.
Carotene is fat-soluble and stable to heat, so it is not lost into cooking water. This is why you should never say that all vitamins are lost in water.

Nutrients are lost in three ways: by dissolving in water (soaking and boiling), by oxidation (reaction with oxygen in the air, at cut surfaces and by enzymes), and by heat (long cooking). Each guideline prevents one of these.
notes.tip: Name the vitamin that is lost, and say why: vitamin C is water-soluble and destroyed by heat and oxidation. Carotene is not lost into water.

notes.h: Guidelines for preparing fruit and vegetables
notes.b: Most nutrient loss starts before the food reaches the pot. Careful preparation keeps the cut surfaces small, the time short and the contact with water to a minimum.
points: Use fresh vegetables that have been stored for as short a time as possible, because vitamin C falls during storage.
Eat fruit and vegetables raw where possible, for example in salads and as raw fruit, because there are then no cooking losses.
Prepare vegetables just before cooking and never leave them standing. Cut surfaces are exposed to air and enzymes, so vitamin C is oxidised the longer they wait.
Use a sharp knife or peeler, because a blunt knife crushes cells and releases oxidase (an enzyme that destroys vitamin C). It also removes less tissue and causes less cell damage.
Cut into large pieces rather than small ones, because small pieces expose more surface to air and water. Large pieces lose fewer nutrients.
Peel thinly, scrape, or leave edible skins on, for example on potatoes, carrots and apples, because nutrients (such as vitamin C in potatoes) and fibre lie close to the skin.

Wash vegetables before cutting, never after, because cut pieces would lose soluble nutrients into the wash water. Do not steep or soak them either, because water-soluble vitamins and minerals leach out.
Remove only inedible or damaged parts. Keep the outer green leaves of greens if they are edible, because they contain more vitamin C and carotene.
notes.tip: Exams ask for guidelines for preparing vegetables, and want a reason with each: for example, sharp knife because blunt tools crush cells, wash before cutting, and no soaking. Large pieces lose less than small ones, so never suggest chopping finely.

notes.b: Once the vegetables are in the pot, the aim is to use as little water, heat and time as possible. Each rule below cuts one of the three routes of nutrient loss.
points: Cook for the shortest time that makes vegetables tender but slightly crisp (al dente, meaning firm to the bite), because overcooking destroys vitamins and spoils texture and flavour.

When boiling, use the minimum amount of water, bring it to the boil before adding the vegetables, and use a tight-fitting lid. Less water means less dissolving, and the lid keeps steam in and shortens cooking time.

Prefer steaming, pressure cooking, microwaving or stir-frying to boiling, as these cooking methods retain most nutrients. Steaming and microwaving give less contact with water, and pressure cooking, microwaving and stir-frying give a shorter cooking time.
In stir-frying, small pieces cooked quickly in a little oil keep their colour, crispness and vitamins, and fat-soluble vitamins (A, carotene and K) are absorbed better with fat.
Microwaving keeps vitamin C only when it is used with very little water and a short cooking time.
Do not add bicarbonate of soda (bread soda) to keep greens green. It destroys vitamin C and thiamine and makes the texture mushy.
Avoid copper and brass pans, because they speed up the destruction of vitamin C.

Cook frozen vegetables from frozen without thawing, to avoid loss of vitamins in the drip liquid. Serve immediately and do not keep them hot for long, because vitamin C falls on holding, and use the cooking liquid in soups, sauces and gravy so the dissolved vitamins and minerals are eaten.
notes.tip: The standard question asks for four guidelines for preparing and cooking vegetables (or three, with one on preparation and one on cooking). Give a reason for each, for example minimum water and tight lid, no bicarbonate of soda because it destroys vitamin C, no copper pans, and keep the cooking liquid.

notes.h: Effects of cooking on nutrients and digestibility
notes.b: Cooking costs some nutrients but gives something back. Heat and water remove the fragile vitamins, while the nutrients that survive can become easier to use.
points: Heat and water destroy or remove vitamin C and the B vitamins (thiamine, riboflavin and folate). The longer the boiling, the greater the loss, because more is destroyed by heat and more dissolves into the water.
Minerals dissolve into the cooking water, which is why the cooking liquid is worth keeping.
Carotene and fibre are kept in cooking, because carotene is stable to heat and fibre is not dissolved by water.
Cooking makes some nutrients more available, because carotene is released from the cell walls and the starch in potatoes and pulses is cooked.

Cooking softens the cellulose and pectin (the materials that hold plant cells together) in the cell walls. Starch in potatoes and pulses swells as it takes up water and softens (gelatinisation). Both changes make the food easier to digest.
Cooking also makes food safer, because it destroys many micro-organisms and denatures (permanently changes the shape of) enzymes.
notes.tip: When asked to outline the effects of cooking on vegetables, cover several effects: starch softens, cellulose softens, micro-organisms are destroyed, enzymes are denatured, colour, flavour and texture change, water-soluble vitamins are lost, vitamin C is destroyed and digestibility improves.

notes.b: The colour of a vegetable comes from pigments, and each pigment reacts to heat, acid and alkali in its own way. Knowing which does what explains why some vegetables stay bright and others dull.
points: Green vegetables owe their colour to chlorophyll. When overcooked or cooked in acid, chlorophyll turns to pheophytin, an olive-green or olive-brown pigment, which is why overcooked cabbage looks dull.
Alkali such as bicarbonate of soda keeps the green colour, but it is harmful to vitamins, so it should not be used.

Orange, yellow and red vegetables such as carrots, peppers and tomatoes contain carotenoid pigments (such as beta-carotene). These are stable in heat, so these vegetables keep their colour when cooked.
Red cabbage contains anthocyanin pigments, which are red in acid and blue or purple in alkaline conditions. Adding vinegar or apple helps to keep red cabbage red when it is cooked.
notes.tip: Learn the colour changes as pairs: chlorophyll goes olive-brown in acid or overcooking, and anthocyanin is red in acid and blue or purple in alkali. Bicarbonate keeps greens green but destroys vitamin C.

notes.h: Effects of cooking on texture and flavour
notes.b: Cooking changes how vegetables feel and taste. Short cooking keeps both at their best, and long cooking spoils them.
points: Texture softens as the cell walls (cellulose and pectin) break down and water is lost or taken up. Overcooked vegetables become mushy, while vegetables cooked briefly keep a crisp texture.
Acid keeps fruit and vegetables firm.
Volatile flavour compounds (flavours that evaporate easily) and water-soluble flavours pass into the cooking water or escape in steam, so long boiling loses flavour.
Overcooked cabbage and other brassicas release sulphur compounds, which give a strong, unpleasant smell.
Roasting or frying brings out sweetness and browning, because the natural sugars in onions and carrots brown in dry heat (caramelisation).
notes.tip: Link each change to a cause: mushy texture comes from broken-down cell walls, lost flavour from boiling for too long, and the strong smell from overcooked brassicas.

notes.b: Blanching is a quick treatment that stops a vegetable changing, and it is carried out before freezing.
points: Blanching means putting prepared vegetables into boiling water for a short time (a minute or a few) and then cooling them quickly in cold water.
It inactivates (denatures) enzymes, which would otherwise carry on working and spoil the food in the freezer.
It also fixes the bright colour of the vegetable, and removes some micro-organisms and air from the surface as a small extra benefit.
Blanching is required before home or commercial freezing. Some water-soluble vitamins are lost, which is a necessary cost.
notes.tip: When asked why vegetables are blanched, give enzyme inactivation first, then colour, and mention the small loss of water-soluble vitamins.

notes.b: Fruit follows the same rules as vegetables, because its vitamin C is just as fragile. The best fruit dishes are raw ones.
points: Eat fruit raw wherever possible, because cooked fruit loses more vitamin C than raw fruit.
Leave the skin on if it is edible, as with apples and pears, or peel thinly, because vitamin C and fibre are kept. Wash rather than peel.
Prepare fruit just before cooking or eating, using a sharp knife, to limit the time its cut surfaces are exposed to air.
Stew fruit in as little water as possible, with a lid, for the shortest time, to limit vitamin C loss and keep its texture. Use the juice, so dissolved nutrients are eaten.
Avoid copper pans, do not overcook, and serve promptly.

Cut apples, pears and bananas brown through enzymic oxidation. Lemon juice or another acid, a sugar syrup or cold water slows browning, which is why a fruit salad is dressed with lemon or orange juice.
notes.tip: The fruit question asks for three guidelines, and each needs a reason: raw or skin on to keep vitamin C and fibre, a little water and a lid for stewing, and lemon juice to slow browning.

keyTerms.definition: A vitamin, such as vitamin C or a B vitamin, that dissolves in water and is lost into cooking water or drip liquid.
A vitamin, such as vitamin A, D, E or K, that dissolves in fat and is not lost into cooking water.
The loss of soluble nutrients and minerals from food into the water used to wash, soak or cook it.
Brief immersion of vegetables in boiling water followed by rapid cooling, to prepare them for freezing.
The swelling of starch granules in hot water, which softens the food and makes starch digestible.
The browning and flavour change that occurs when natural sugars are heated strongly.
The green pigment in vegetables, which changes to an olive-brown colour when overcooked or cooked in acid.
Cooked until still slightly firm to the bite, which keeps texture and reduces nutrient loss.

factCards.term: Four cooking methods that retain most nutrients
factCards.definition: Steaming, microwaving with very little water for a short time, stir-frying and boiling in the minimum amount of water with a lid.

factCards.term: Why bicarbonate of soda should not be added to vegetable cooking water
factCards.definition: It destroys vitamin C and softens the texture, although it keeps the vegetables green.

factCards.term: Three purposes of blanching before freezing
factCards.definition: Denatures enzymes, fixes bright colour, and reduces micro-organisms on the surface.

factCards.term: Three causes of vitamin C loss in cooking
factCards.definition: Heat, oxidation and leaching into cooking water.
Carotene is fat-soluble and stable to heat, so it is not lost into cooking water.

factCards.term: Colour change of chlorophyll in acid
factCards.definition: Chlorophyll converts to pheophytin, turning the vegetable olive-brown.

factCards.term: Starch change in potatoes on heating
factCards.definition: Gelatinisation: starch granules swell and absorb water, softening the potato.

factCards.term: Why copper and brass pans are avoided for vegetables
factCards.definition: They speed up the destruction of vitamin C during cooking.

questions.prompt: State two reasons why vegetables should be prepared shortly before they are cooked.
questions.model: Any two: cutting exposes more surface to air, so vitamin C is oxidised and destroyed; standing in water or soaking lets water-soluble vitamins and minerals leach out; enzymes and browning reactions begin once cells are damaged.

questions.prompt: Explain how preparation and cooking affect the nutritive value, colour, texture and flavour of green vegetables, and recommend a method of cooking that keeps most of their nutrients.
questions.model: Nutritive value: vitamin C is lost through cutting, soaking, heat, oxidation and leaching into cooking water; water-soluble B vitamins and folate leach out and are reduced by prolonged heat. Colour: chlorophyll turns olive-brown with overcooking or in acid, and bicarbonate of soda keeps green colour only by destroying vitamin C. Texture: heat softens cellulose and pectin, so overcooked vegetables become mushy. Flavour: volatile compounds escape in steam and sulphur compounds in brassicas produce strong odours when overcooked. Recommended method: wash before cutting, prepare just before cooking, use large pieces, then steam, microwave or stir-fry, or boil in the minimum water with a tight lid for the minimum time, serve immediately and use any cooking liquid in soups or sauces.
